THOUGHT: The infant’s age (9 months) and the sequence of events are classic for roseola (exanthem subitum): several days of high fever (40.5°C) often with febrile seizures in this age group, followed by abrupt defervescence and development of a nonpruritic, blanching maculopapular rash that begins on the trunk and spreads to the extremities. Normal CBC and well appearance now fit a self-limited viral illness. Alternative diagnoses (measles, rubella, parvovirus, enteroviral exanthems) are less likely because measles typically has prodromal cough/coryza/conjunctivitis and Koplik spots with rash starting on the face; rubella causes milder fever and while it can cause posterior auricular adenopathy, it does not classically follow high fever with febrile seizure; parvovirus has a different rash pattern. Posterior auricular lymphadenopathy can be seen with viral infections and does not override the overall clinical picture. Therefore the most likely diagnosis is roseola (HHV-6/7) with a febrile seizure during the febrile phase.

DIAGNOSIS: Roseola infantum (exanthem subitum due to HHV‑6/7) with a febrile seizure.
